summary: For the period 2025-06-30 to 2026-06-30, the business processed 817 total orders generating net revenue of $233,944.75 (after $19,135.25 in discounts off $253,080.00 gross revenue), with an average net order value of $286.35 and a gross margin of 35.09% (calculated on the net-revenue basis). Sports led category performance with $64,898.75 in net revenue, while Electronics lagged at $28,220.50.
risks: Nearly a quarter of orders (24.98%, 272 of the orders tracked) were cancelled, which materially shrinks realized revenue and may signal fulfillment, pricing, or product-fit problems.
Discounting removed $19,135.25 from gross revenue, a meaningful gap between gross and net revenue that should be monitored for margin erosion.
Electronics is significantly underperforming the top category (Sports) in net revenue, indicating concentration risk if Sports demand softens.

The reported repeat-customer rate of 100% alongside only 100 total customers looks implausible for a real e-commerce business and should be treated as a data-quality issue rather than a genuine performance signal before it informs any retention strategy.

recommendations.text: Investigate the root causes behind the 272 cancelled orders (24.98% of orders), since reducing cancellations directly protects gross revenue and net revenue.
Review discounting practices, as $19,135.25 in discounts is eroding gross revenue down to net revenue and compressing the margin base used for the 35.09% gross margin figure.

Reassess merchandising and inventory investment in Electronics given its net revenue of $28,220.50 trails well behind the top-performing Sports category's $64,898.75, and consider reallocating marketing spend toward Sports while diagnosing Electronics' weakness.
Continue tracking gross margin (currently 35.09% on a net-revenue basis) against total cost of $151,848.00 to ensure margin does not deteriorate further as order volume or discounting changes.

Before using the repeat-customer rate in any retention or loyalty strategy, validate the underlying customer data, since a 100% repeat rate across 100 total customers is an unusual result that likely reflects a data or definition issue rather than actual behavior.
